sentences: A young woman in a white chemise sits in a large chair.
Her left hand touches her cheek, and her head tilts gently to the right in a pensive expression.
The whole picture flows along soft, unbroken curves, calm and unhurried.
She is Jeanne Hébuterne, a young aspiring artist who met Amedeo Modigliani in March 1917 and became his partner.
He painted her more than twenty times, usually emphasising her thick auburn hair and blue eyes.
Begin with her hair.
Thick auburn locks frame her narrow face and fall toward her shoulders.
That deep colour sharply separates her pale face from the blue wall behind her.
Her face is a long, narrow oval, and the line of her nose runs straight and long.
The eyes are painted in pale blue with no pupils at all.
Because of that, her gaze seems turned inward rather than out toward us.
Now look at the left hand resting on her cheek.
Her arm, draped over the back of the chair, bends up in one long line, and her fingertips lightly support her chin.
The fingers are elongated, just like her face.
Follow the line of her neck and shoulders.
The long neck tilts to one side, and her sloping shoulders carry that line onward.
This gentle slant gives the whole painting a quiet rhythm.
The large chair on the right wraps around her in warm ochre.
White dress, blue wall and ochre chair are laid down as simple fields of colour, giving the composition a firm structure.
Notice, too, the brushstrokes left visible across the surface of the chair.
Lower down, her right hand rests in her lap.
Together with the hand at her cheek, it forms a long diagonal that pulls her body to one side.
Even though she is seated, she seems to be leaning, slowly and gently.
The elongated figure and lopsided composition borrow the exaggerated elegance of sixteenth-century Italian Mannerism.
Born in Livorno, Modigliani moved to Paris in 1906, where he developed his distinctive portraits with long oval faces.
In the upper right you can see Modigliani's signature.
The couple had their daughter on the Côte d'Azur and returned to Paris in May 1919.
He painted this that same year, but afterward his health declined quickly.
He died on 24 January 1920, and Jeanne, pregnant with their second child, died two days later.
Step back one more time, look into those pale, empty eyes, and ask yourself what she might have been thinking.
